'''''Mespilus germanica''''', known as the '''medlar''' or '''common medlar''', is a large [[shrub]] or small tree in the rose family [[Rosaceae]]. When the genus ''[[Mespilus]]'' is included in the genus ''[[Crataegus]]'', the [[correct name]] for this species is '''''Crataegus germanica''''' ([[Carl Linnaeus|L.]]) [[Otto Kuntze|Kuntze]].

The fruit of this tree, also called medlar, has been cultivated since [[Roman era|Roman times]]. It is usually available in winter and eaten when [[Bletting|bletted]]. It may be consumed raw and in a range of cooked dishes.

==Description==
Under ideal circumstances, the [[deciduous]] plant grows up to {{convert|8|m|ft|abbr=off}} tall. Generally, it is shorter and more shrub-like than tree-like. With a lifespan of 30–60 years, the tree is rather short-lived.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|date=2021-05-24|title=The Essential Guide to probably everything you need to know about Growing Medlar – Mespilus germanica|url=https://www.permaculturenews.org/2021/05/24/the-essential-guide-to-probably-everything-you-need-to-know-about-growing-medlar-mespilus-germanica/|access-date=2021-11-14|website=The Permaculture Research Institute|language=en-US}}</ref> Its bark is greyish brown with deep vertical cracks forming rectangular plates that tend to lift off.<ref name=":11" />

The wild form of ''M. germanica'' is mostly a thorny, more shrub-like than tree-like plant, which is between {{convert|1.5|and|4|m|abbr=on|ft|0}} high. In the cultivated forms, the thorns are usually reduced or even completely absent.<ref name=":2" /> In general, the medlar is a small, deciduous tree with an overhanging, almost round crown. The trunk is irregularly shaped.<ref name=":3" /> The tree has a height between {{convert|1|and|6|m|abbr=on|frac=2|ft}}, but can become significantly larger in culture.<ref name=":4" /> The [[diameter at breast height]] is usually between {{convert|20|and|25|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}, but in exceptional cases it can be up to {{convert|50|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}. The roots are heavily branched and far-ranging, with a somewhat [[fibrous root system]].<ref name=":3" />

The wood has a fine texture, but is very hard.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Baird|first1=John R.|last2=Thieret|first2=John W.|date=1989-07-01|title=The medlar (Mespilus germanica, Rosaceae) from antiquity to obscurity|journal=Economic Botany|language=en|volume=43|issue=3|pages=328–372|doi=10.1007/BF02858732|bibcode=1989EcBot..43..328B |s2cid=40866174|issn=1874-9364}}</ref> It has a white, slightly pink-tinted sapwood. The core is brownish. The annual rings are clearly visible.<ref name=":3">{{Citation|last=Minotta|first=Gianfranco|editor1-first=Bernd|editor1-last=Stimm|editor2-first=Andreas|editor2-last=Roloff|editor3-first=Ulla M|editor3-last=Lang|editor4-first=Horst|editor4-last=Weisgerber|chapter=Mespilus germanica|date=2014|chapter-url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/9783527678518.ehg2000006|title=Enzyklopädie der Holzgewächse: Handbuch und Atlas der Dendrologie|pages=1–6|publisher=American Cancer Society|language=de|doi=10.1002/9783527678518|isbn=978-3-527-67851-8|access-date=2021-11-14|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The winter buds are pointed, ovoid and up to {{convert|5|mm|in|frac=4|abbr=off}} long.<ref name=":3" /> The leaves are dark green and elliptic, {{convert|8|–|15|cm|in|0}} long and {{convert|3|–|5|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} wide. The leaves are densely hairy (pubescent) below, and turn red in autumn before falling.<ref name="Mitchell">{{cite book | title=A Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Collins | author=Mitchell, Alan | year=1978 | page=277 | edition=2}}</ref>

Medlar flowers are {{convert|2|–|5|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} in diameter, have a short stalk and are terminal and single on short side shoots. They have five elongated, narrow [[sepals]] and five free, white or pale pink [[petals]].<ref name=":2" /> Compared to other fruit trees in the European latitudes, the medlar flowers very late (May or June).<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Erhaltungskonzept Mispel|url=https://www.infoflora.ch/assets/content/documents/conservation/M_Schmutz_2016_Erhaltungskonzept_Mispel.pdf}}</ref>  The flowers are [[hermaphrodite]] and pollinated by bees.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|title="Mespilus germanica Medlar PFAF Plant Database".|url=https://pfaf.org/user/plant.aspx?LatinName=Mespilus+germanica}}</ref> Normally, [[self-pollination]] occurs in this plant.<ref name=":3" /> The flower then develops flattened, reddish-brown, hairy fruits with juicy flesh.<ref name=":4" /> The reddish-brown fruit is a [[pome]], {{convert|2|–|3|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} diameter, with wide-spreading persistent sepals around a central pit, giving a 'hollow' appearance to the fruit.<ref name="Mitchell" /> In cultivated forms the diameter is even between {{convert|3|and|8|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}}.<ref name=":3" />

[[Sexual reproduction of plants|Sexual reproduction]] is the norm in wild forms of the medlar. The resulting seeds have a [[germination]] capacity lasting from 18 to 20 months. The seeds are distributed by various animals such as birds, squirrels and deer. Some [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] are sterile and can therefore only be propagated [[vegetatively]].<ref name=":4" />

The number of [[chromosomes]] is given as 2n = 32 or 2n = 34.<ref name=":2" />

Until recently, ''M. germanica'' was the only known species of medlar. However, in 1990, a new species was discovered in North America, now named ''[[Mespilus canescens|M. canescens]]''. The [[loquat]], ''Eriobotrya japonica'', is more distantly related to the medlar than genera such as ''[[Crataegus]]'', ''[[Amelanchier]]'', ''[[Peraphyllum]]'', and ''[[Malacomeles]]'',<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Campbell, C.S. |author2=Evans, R.C. |author3=Morgan, D.R. |author4=Dickinson, T.A. |author5=Arsenault, M.P. |year=2007 |title=Phylogeny of subtribe Pyrinae (formerly the Maloideae, Rosaceae): Limited resolution of a complex evolutionary history |url=http://biology.umaine.edu/Amelanchier/Pyrinae_2007.pdf |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |volume=266 |issue=1–2 |pages=119–145 |doi=10.1007/s00606-007-0545-y |bibcode=2007PSyEv.266..119C |s2cid=13639534}}</ref> but was once thought to be closely related, and is still sometimes called the 'Chinese medlar' or 'Japanese medlar'.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Die Asperl Mespilus germanica L. |date=2013 |others=Georg Schramayr, Verein Regionale Gehölzvermehrung |isbn=978-3-901542-41-1 |location=St. Pölten |oclc=967971863}}</ref>

=== Systematics ===
Within the species ''M. germanica'' 23 [[Taxon|taxa]] are distinguished, also comprising wild or semi-wild forms, ornamental and of different origin.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cristofori |first1=V. |last2=Silvestri |first2=C. |last3=Pica |first3=A.L. |last4=Bertazza |first4=G. |last5=Bignami |first5=C. |date=2019-12-29 |title=Evaluation of four medlar cultivars: agronomical, pomological and qualitative traits |journal=European Journal of Horticultural Science |volume=84 |issue=6 |pages=350–358 |doi=10.17660/ejhs.2019/84.6.4 |issn=1611-4426 |s2cid=214450102|doi-access=free |hdl=11380/1200235 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Among them there are the following varieties:<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Schmid |first1=Rudolf |last2=Phipps |first2=James B. |last3=O'Kennon |first3=Robert J. |last4=Lance |first4=Ron W. |date=November 2003 |title=Hawthorns and Medlars |journal=Taxon |volume=52 |issue=4 |page=884 |doi=10.2307/3647377 |jstor=3647377 |bibcode=2003Taxon..52S.884S }}</ref>
* ''Mespilus germanica'' var. ''gigantea'' [[Oskar von Kirchner|Kirchn]]. with very large fruits
* ''Mespilus germanica'' var. ''abortiva'' Kirchn. with fruits without seeds
* ''Mespilus germanica'' var. ''argenteo-variegata'' with white variegated leaves as ornamental plant
* ''Mespilus germanica'' var. ''aureo-variegata'' with yellow variegated leaves as ornamental plant

[[Cultivar]]s of ''M. germanica'' that are grown for their fruit include 'Hollandia', 'Nottingham', and 'Russian',<ref name=":9" /> the large-fruited variety 'Dutch' (also known as 'Giant' or 'Monstrous'), 'Breda giant', 'Large Russian',<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lothian |first=Thomas |title=The complete book of fruit growing in Australia. |year=1991 |location=Port Melbourne, Victoria}}</ref> 'Royal' with very high yield,<ref name=":3b">{{Cite book |last=Schütt |title=Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume |page=336}}</ref> 'Early medlar' with early ripening and high quality fruits, 'Seedless' with seedless fruits of low quality.

The cultivar 'Nottingham' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHSPF">{{cite web |title=RHS Plantfinder – ''Mespilus germanica'' 'Nottingham' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/64367/i-Mespilus-germanica-i-Nottingham-(F)/Details |access-date=4 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=July 2017 |title=AGM Plants – Ornamental |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |access-date=4 April 2018 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |page=64}}</ref>

For a time it was assumed that it was a species with narrow [[genetic resources]] and therefore subject to high risks of genetic erosion, whereby the limited evolution of ''M. germanica'' diversity was ascribed to the lack of economic interest for this fruit species in the last centuries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dipartimento di Scienze Agrarie e Forestali, Università degli Studi della Tuscia, Viterbo, Italy |last2=Cristofori |first2=V. |last3=Silvestri |first3=C. |last4=Dipartimento di Scienze Agrarie e Forestali, Università degli Studi della Tuscia, Viterbo, Italy |last5=Pica |first5=A.L. |last6=Dipartimento di Scienze Agrarie e Forestali, Università degli Studi della Tuscia, Viterbo, Italy |last7=Bertazza |first7=G. |last8=Istituto di Biometeorologia, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche, Bologna, Italy |last9=Bignami |first9=C. |last10=Dipartimento di Scienze della Vita, Università degli Studi di Modena e Reggio Emilia, Reggio Emilia, Italy |date=2019-12-29 |title=Evaluation of four medlar cultivars: agronomical, pomological and qualitative traits |url=https://www.pubhort.org/ejhs/84/6/4/index.htm |journal=European Journal of Horticultural Science |volume=84 |issue=6 |pages=350–358 |doi=10.17660/eJHS.2019/84.6.4 |s2cid=214450102|doi-access=free |hdl=11380/1200235 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> However, current findings show that natural populations of medlar are diverse with a high genetic potential, which could be used to improve production by using specific genotypes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baird |first1=John R. |last2=Thieret |first2=John W. |date=July 1989 |title=The medlar (Mespilus germanica, Rosaceae) from antiquity to obscurity |journal=Economic Botany |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=328–372 |doi=10.1007/bf02858732 |bibcode=1989EcBot..43..328B |issn=0013-0001 |s2cid=40866174}}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
The Latin name {{lang|la|germanica}} means 'German', although the species is indigenous to other areas.<ref name="Baird">{{cite journal |last1=Baird |first1=J. R. |last2=Thieret |first2=J. W. |year=1989 |title=The Medlar (''Mespilus germanica'', Rosaceae) from antiquity to obscurity |journal=Economic Botany |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=328–372 |doi=10.1007/BF02858732 |jstor=4255177 |bibcode=1989EcBot..43..328B |s2cid=40866174}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
From an extensive study of literature and plant specimens, {{ill|Kazimierz Browicz|pl}}<ref name="Baird" /> concluded that the true homeland of ''M. germanica'' is only in the southeastern part of the Balkan peninsula, in [[Asia Minor]], on the [[Caucasus]], [[Crimea]], northern [[Iran]], and possibly also in [[Turkmenistan]]. It is also found in [[southeastern Europe]], especially the [[Black Sea]] coasts of [[Bulgaria]] and [[Turkey]].<ref name="Baird" /> Fossil remains, however, have been reported from a wider area, including from Oriolo, Italy ({{Circa|800}} kya thousand years ago) and Burgtonna, Germany (130-115 thousand years ago), dating from the [[Pleistocene]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Spengler |first1=Robert N. |last2=Kienast |first2=Frank |last3=Roberts |first3=Patrick |last4=Boivin |first4=Nicole |last5=Begun |first5=David R. |last6=Ashastina |first6=Kseniia |last7=Petraglia |first7=Michael |date=2023-06-01 |title=Bearing Fruit: Miocene Apes and Rosaceous Fruit Evolution |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s13752-022-00413-1 |journal=Biological Theory |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=134–151 |doi=10.1007/s13752-022-00413-1 |issn=1555-5550 |pmc=10191964 |pmid=37214192}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Denk |first1=Thomas |last2=Sami |first2=Marco |last3=Teodoridis |first3=Vasilis |last4=Martinetto |first4=Edoardo |date=2022 |title=The late Early Pleistocene flora of Oriolo, Faenza (Italy): assembly of the modern forest biome |url=http://fi.nm.cz/en/clanek/the-late-early-pleistocene-flora-of-oriolo-faenza-italy-assembly-of-the-modern-forest-biome-2/ |journal=Fossil Imprint |language=en |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=217–262 |doi=10.37520/fi.2022.009 |doi-access=free |issn=2533-4069}}</ref>

The species requires [[temperate]] and [[Mediterranean climate|sub-mediterranean]] climate conditions with warm summers and mild winters.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Clarke |first=Richard |date=October 1982 |title=The Trees of Britain and Northern Europe, by Alan Mitchell and John Wilkinson Collins Pocket Guides, £6.95 hardback, £3.95 paperback. |journal=Oryx |language=en |volume=16 |issue=5 |page=457 |doi=10.1017/S0030605300018226 |s2cid=84855677 |issn=0030-6053|doi-access=free }}</ref> Air temperatures of {{convert|18|to|20|°C|0|abbr=on}} are mentioned as favourable for growth, cold of as low as {{convert|-20|°C|0|abbr=on}} is tolerated and late frosts hardly cause any damage. The wild form was observed in dry areas with annual precipitation of {{convert|700|mm|in|abbr=on}} and at altitudes from {{convert|0|to|1100|m|-2|abbr=on}}. The species grows in a wide range of soil types and prefers fresh, well-drained loamy soils with a [[Soil pH|pH]] that is between 6 and 8.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Khadivi |first1=Ali |last2=Rezaei |first2=Mehdi |last3=Heidari |first3=Parviz |last4=Safari-Khuzani |first4=Amir |last5=Sahebi |first5=Mohammad |date=June 2019 |title=Morphological and fruit characterizations of common medlar (Mespilus germanica L.) germplasm |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |volume=252 |pages=38–47 |doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2019.03.014 |bibcode=2019ScHor.252...38K |issn=0304-4238 |s2cid=146091508}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume |publisher=Schütt et al. |page=337}}</ref> <!-- the following two sentences are self contradictory and need clarifying on the basis of more sources -->It is found across southern Europe where it is generally rare. It is reported to be naturalised in some woods in southeast England, but is found in few gardens.<ref name="Mitchell" />

== Ecology ==

=== Plant disease ===
''M. germanica'' is only rarely attacked by diseases or harmed by insects.<ref name=":3" />

In plantations, the larvae of the leaf-mining butterfly species ''Lithocolletis blancardella'' can cause damage. Furthermore, especially in years with high precipitation, the fungus ''[[Monilinia fructigena]]'' can be a problem.<ref name=":3" /> It causes brown blemishes on the fruit and continues to spread until the fruit becomes entirely rotten.<ref name=":5" />

''M. germanica'' can also be infected by ''[[Podosphaera clandestina var. clandestina|Podosphaera clandestina]]'', the pathogen of [[powdery mildew]], which can lead to the wilting of leaves and buds as well as by ''Entomosporium mespili'' that causes leaf spots.<ref name=":3" />

The medlar is, like other species of the rosacea family which are used for propagation, susceptible to ''[[Erwinia|Erwinia amylovora]]'', the parasitic causative agent of [[fire blight]].<ref name=":3" />

== Cultivation ==
The species may have been cultivated for as long as 3,000 years.<ref name="Baird" /> The ancient Greek geographer [[Strabo]] refers to a {{lang|grc|μέσπιλον}} ({{lang|grc-Latn|méspilon}}) in ''[[Geographica]]'', Book 16, Chapter 4.<ref>{{cite web |title=Perseus Search Results |url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/searchresults?q=me/spilon&target=greek&doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0197&expand=lemma&sort=docorder |website=www.perseus.tufts.edu}}</ref> The medlar was introduced to Greece around 700 BC and to [[Roman Empire|Rome]] about 200 BC. It was an important fruit plant during Roman and medieval times. By the 17th and 18th centuries, however, it had been superseded by other fruits, and is cultivated much less today.<ref name="BBC"/>

''M. germanica'' pomes are one of the few fruits that become edible in winter, making it an important tree for [[gardener]]s who wish to have fruit available all year round.<ref name="RHSadvice">{{cite web |date=2011 |title=Medlar |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/AdviceSearch/profile.aspx?pid=131 |access-date=8 July 2013 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society}}</ref>

Cultivated forms are propagated by [[inoculation]] and by [[grafting]] on various substrates such as ''[[Crataegus]]'' (hawthorn) species, [[mountain ash]], [[pear]] or [[quince]] to improve the performance in different soils.<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RHSadvice" /> Cultivars reach full fruit set 6 to 7 years after grafting and they keep it for 20 to 25 years. The fruit production varies between {{convert|30|and|70|kg|-1|abbr=off}} per tree and year, depending on the variety and age.<ref name=":3" />

Grafting on medlar seedlings is not recommended because of the slow growth of the grafts. Irrigation and fertilisation can stimulate growth in plantations.<ref name=":3" /> If the fruit-bearing shoots are cut back after the harvest, the formation of new fertile short shoots is encouraged.<ref name=":3" />

== Uses ==
[[File:Mespilus germanica ripening process.jpg|thumb|[[Bletting]] begins on one side of the fruit. Bletted flesh is brown; ripe but unbletted flesh is white.|alt=Fruit cut in half showing brown 'bletting' which makes it edible]] The fruits are hard and acidic even when ripe, but become edible after being softened, "[[Bletting|bletted]]", by frost,<ref name="BBC">{{cite news |author=Gorvett, Zaria |date=25 March 2021 |title=The forgotten medieval fruit with a vulgar name |url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20210325-the-strange-medieval-fruit-the-world-forgot |access-date=10 October 2024 |work=[[BBC News Online]]}}</ref> or naturally in storage if given sufficient time by reducing [[tannin]] content and fruit acids, increasing sugar content, and changes in the content of minerals.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=Glew|first1=Robert H.|last2=Ayaz|first2=Faik A.|last3=Sanz|first3=Carlos|last4=VanderJagt|first4=D.J.|last5=Huang|first5=H.-S.|last6=Chuang|first6=L.-T.|last7=Strnad|first7=M.|title=Changes in sugars, organic acids and amino acids in medlar (''Mespilus germanica'' L.) during fruit development and maturation|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0308814603000979|journal=Food Chemistry|language=en|volume=83|issue=3|pages=363–369|date=1 November 2003|doi=10.1016/S0308-8146(03)00097-9|bibcode=2003FoodC..83..363G |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Once softening begins, the skin rapidly takes on a wrinkled texture and turns dark brown, and the inside reduces to the consistency and flavour reminiscent of [[apple sauce]]. This process can confuse those new to medlars, as its softened fruit looks as if it has spoiled.<ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rop|first1=Otakar|last2=Sochor|first2=Jiri|last3=Jurikova|first3=Tunde|last4=Zitka|first4=Ondrej|last5=Skutkova|first5=Helena|last6=Mlcek|first6=Jiri|last7=Salas|first7=Petr|last8=Krska|first8=Boris|last9=Babula|first9=Petr|last10=Adam|first10=Vojtech|last11=Kramarova|first11=Daniela|date=2010-12-28|title=Effect of Five Different Stages of Ripening on Chemical Compounds in Medlar (Mespilus germanica L.)|journal=Molecules|language=en|volume=16|issue=1|pages=74–91|doi=10.3390/molecules16010074|issn=1420-3049|pmc=6259355|pmid=21189456|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In [[Gilan]], northern [[Iran]], the leaves, bark, fruits and wood of the medlar tree are traditionally used in herbal medicine.<ref name="BBC" />

=== Product use ===
Once bletted, the fruit can be eaten raw, sometimes with sugar and cream—it has been described as being an "acquired taste"<ref name=BBCdessert>{{cite web | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/food/medlars | title=Medlars recipes | publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation | access-date=8 July 2013 | author=Martin, James}}</ref>—or used to make medlar [[Fruit preserves#Jelly|jelly]].<ref name=SlaterRHS>{{cite web | url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/Gardening/Grow-Your-Own/Recipes/Nigel-Slater-recipes/Articles/Nigel-Slater-On---/Nigel-Slater-on----medlars | title=Nigel Slater on... medlars | publisher=Royal Horticultural Society | access-date=8 July 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121013231447/http://www.rhs.org.uk/Gardening/Grow-Your-Own/Recipes/Nigel-Slater-recipes/Articles/Nigel-Slater-On---/Nigel-Slater-on----medlars | archive-date=13 October 2012 }}</ref> It is used in "medlar cheese", which is similar to [[lemon curd]], made with the fruit pulp, eggs, and butter.<ref name=BBCdessert/>

Unripe fruits have a relatively high tannin content of about 2.6% and are therefore used for [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]]. The tannin causes [[flocculation]] of proteins, enabling its use to reduce the [[turbidity]] of wine. In [[Saarland]], Germany, a [[schnapps]] is made from the fruit of the medlar, which is refined with [[Crataegus|hawthorn]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Lehnert|first=Charly|title=Das saarländische Geheichnis Bd. 1|date=2014|isbn=978-3-939286-18-9|location=Saarbrücken|oclc=892065284}}</ref> "Medlar tea" usually is not made from ''M. germanica'', but from [[wolfberry]], or goji, which is sometimes inaccurately translated as "red medlar."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3344996/Goji-berries-The-new-superfruit.html | title=Goji berries: The new superfruit | publisher=The (Daily) Telegraph | date=12 October 2007 | access-date=8 July 2013 | author=McAdam, Diana}}</ref>

''Mespilus germanica'' kernel oil was used for the first time to produce [[biodiesel]], whereby [[linoleic acid]] and [[oleic acid]] with about 40% are main constituents of the extracted oil. The physical properties of the produced biodiesel allows an alternative for diesel fuels without any modification to the conventional engines.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Qasemi|first1=Zeinab|last2=Jafari|first2=Dariush|last3=Jafari|first3=Kourosh|last4=Esmaeili|first4=Hossein|date=2021-08-23|title=Heterogeneous aluminum oxide/calcium oxide catalyzed transesterification of Mespilus germanica triglyceride for biodiesel production|journal=Environmental Progress & Sustainable Energy|volume=41 |issue=2 |article-number=e13738 |doi=10.1002/ep.13738|s2cid=238740226|issn=1944-7442}}</ref> Leaves of medlar fruit were used to produce activated carbon to remove [[heavy metals]] like Ni<sup>2+</sup> from aqueous solutions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Khedri|first1=Ali|last2=Jafari|first2=Dariush|last3=Esfandyari|first3=Morteza|date=2021-07-27|title=Adsorption of Nickel(II) Ions from Synthetic Wastewater Using Activated Carbon Prepared from Mespilus germanica Leaf|journal=[[Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering]]|volume=47 |issue=5 |pages=6155–6166 |doi=10.1007/s13369-021-06014-7|s2cid=237723962|issn=2193-567X}}</ref>

Silver [[nanoparticle]]s could be synthesised from ''M. germanica'' extract and show antibacterial, [[Biofilm|antibiofilm]] activities against multidrug resistance of ''[[Klebsiella pneumoniae]]'' clinical strains.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Foroohimanjili|first1=Fatemeh|last2=Mirzaie|first2=Amir|last3=Hamdi|first3=Seyed Mohammad Mehdi|last4=Noorbazargan|first4=Hassan|last5=Hedayati Ch|first5=Mojtaba|last6=Dolatabadi|first6=Aghigh|last7=Rezaie|first7=Hossein|last8=Bishak|first8=Faezeh M.|date=2020-01-29|title=Antibacterial, antibiofilm, and antiquorum sensing activities of phytosynthesized silver nanoparticles fabricated from ''Mespilus germanica'' extract against multidrug resistance of ''Klebsiella pneumoniae'' clinical strains|journal=Journal of Basic Microbiology|volume=60|issue=3|pages=216–230|doi=10.1002/jobm.201900511|pmid=31994223|s2cid=210949728|issn=0233-111X}}</ref>

=== Nutrients and phytochemicals ===
In general, the medlar fruits were found to be rich in potassium, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium and iron.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|last=D.|first=Ercisli, S. Sengul, M. Yildiz, H. Sener, D. Duralija, B. Voca, S. Dujmovic Purgar|title=Phytochemical and antioxidant characteristics of medlar fruits (Mespilus germanica L.)|date=2012-10-16|publisher=Journal of Applied Botany and Food Quality|oclc=825218272}}</ref>

''M. germanica'' contains various [[phytochemical]]s varying between genotypes,<ref name=":7" /> fruit ripeness, harvest time and storage conditions. The fruits are particularly rich in [[monoterpene]]s and [[organic acid]]s.<ref name=":10" /><ref>G. Bounous, E. Zanini: ''Variabilità di alcune componenti e caratteri biometrici dei frutti di 6 specie arboree ed arbustive''. Proc. workshop "Lampone mirtillo ed altri piccoli frutti", Trento, 1987, 189–197 (Zitiert nach Schuck et al.: ''Enzyklopädie der Laubbäume'').</ref> Amino acids, sugars, and organic acids affect flavour.<ref name=":10" />

Due to their [[diuretic]] and [[astringent]] effects, the fruits have been used in [[traditional medicine]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Peyre|title=Les Arbres & Leurs Fruits, Usage Medicaux Pharmaceutiques & Dietetiques.|year=1945}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{citation|surname1=Steffen Guido Fleischhauer, Jürgen Guthmann, Roland Spiegelberger|title=Essbare Wildpflanzen 200 Arten bestimmen und verwenden|edition=17. Auflage|publisher=AT Verlag|at=p. 69|isbn=978-3-03800-886 6|date=2015|language=German}}</ref>

==In culture==
[[File:Mispel jm55216 (cropped).jpg|thumb|A basket of medlars]]
[[File:Mespilus Ibn Butlan.jpg|thumb|Medlars depicted in [[Tacuinum Sanitatis]], 14th century]]

===Chaucer===
A fruit which is rotten before it is ripe, the medlar is used figuratively in literature as a symbol of [[prostitution]] or premature destitution. For example, in the Prologue to ''[[The Reeve's Tale]]'', [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s character laments his old age, comparing himself to the medlar, which he names using the [[Middle English]] term for the fruit, "open-arse":
{{Blockquote|
:This white top writeth myne olde yeris;
:Myn herte is mowled also as myne heris —
:But if I fare as dooth an open-ers.
:That ilke fruyt is ever lenger the wers,
:Til it be roten in mullok or in stree.
:We olde men, I drede, so fare we:
:Til we be roten, kan we nat be rype;}}

===Shakespeare===
In [[William Shakespeare]]'s ''[[Timon of Athens]]'', [[Apemantus]] forces an apple upon [[Timon of Athens (person)|Timon]]: "The middle of humanity thou never knewest, but the extremity of both ends. When thou wast in thy gilt and perfume, they mock'd thee for too much curiosity; in thy rags thou know'st none, but art despised for the contrary. There's a medlar for thee; eat it", perhaps including a pun on "meddler", one who meddles in affairs, as well as on rottenness. (IV.iii.300–305).

In ''[[Measure for Measure]]'', Lucio excuses his denial of past fornication because "they would else have married me to the rotten medlar." (IV.iii.171).

In ''[[As You Like It]]'', Rosalind makes a complicated pun involving grafting her interlocutor with the trees around her which bear love letters and with a medlar: "I'll graff it with you, and then I shall graff it with a medlar. Then it will be the earliest fruit i' th' country; for you'll be rotten ere you be half ripe, and that's the right virtue of the medlar."  (III.ii.116–119).

The most famous reference to medlars, often [[bowdlerized]] until modern editions accepted it, appears in Shakespeare's ''[[Romeo and Juliet]]'', when Mercutio laughs at Romeo's unrequited love for his mistress Rosaline (II, 1, 34–38):
{{Blockquote|
:Now will he sit under a medlar tree,
:And wish his mistress were that kind of fruit
:As maids call medlars, when they laugh alone.
:O Romeo, that she were, O that she were
:An open-arse and thou a pop'rin pear!}}
In the 16th and 17th centuries, medlars were bawdily called "open-arses" because of the shape of the fruits — a name that first appears in [[Old English]] as ''openærs''<ref>''Oxford English Dictionary'', “open-arse (''n.''),” December 2025, https://doi.org/10.1093/OED/6270407864.</ref> — inspiring boisterous or humorously indecent puns in many [[English Renaissance theatre|Elizabethan and Jacobean plays]]. The name survived in common use well into the 20th century.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=MacMillan |first=Alexander Stuart |title=Popular Names of Flowers, Fruits, &C: As Used in the County of Somerset and the Adjacent Parts of Devon, Dorset and Wilts |date=1922 |publisher=Forgotten Books |isbn=1-332-98501-7 |location=United Kingdom |page=209 |oclc=978686284}}</ref> In the southwest of England it was historically called '''monkey's bottom''', due to the appearance of its large calyx (sepals).

===Other 16th- and 17th-century authors===
In [[Miguel de Cervantes]]' [[Don Quixote]] the eponymous hero and Sancho Panza "stretch themselves out in the middle of a field and stuff themselves with acorns or medlars."

In [[François Rabelais]]' [[Gargantua and Pantagruel]], medlars play a role in the origin of giants, including the eponymous characters. After [[Cain]] killed [[Abel]], the blood of the just saturated the Earth, causing enormous medlars to grow. Humans who ate these medlars grew to great proportions. Those whose bodies grew longer became giants, and were the ancestors of Gargantua and Pantagruel.

[[Thomas Dekker (poet)|Thomas Dekker]] also draws a comparison in his play ''[[The Honest Whore]]'': "I scarce know her, for the beauty of her cheek hath, like the moon, suffered strange eclipses since I beheld it: women are like medlars, no sooner ripe but rotten."

Another reference can be found in [[Thomas Middleton]]'s ''A Trick to Catch the Old One'' in the character of Widow Medler, impersonated by a courtesan, hence the following pun: "Who? Widow Medler? She lies open to much rumour."<ref>II, 2, 59.</ref>

In the Memoirs of [[Glückel of Hameln]], Glückel recalls having had a craving for medlars when she was pregnant with her son Joseph, but ignoring the desire. When the baby was born, he was sickly and too weak to be breastfed. Remembering a superstition about the dangers of pregnant women not fulfilling their cravings, Glückel asked for someone to fetch her some medlars for the baby. As soon as the fruit touched the baby's lips, he ate all the pulp given to him, and was then able to be breastfed.<ref>Book 4, Section 14.</ref>

===Modern literature===
In modern literature, some writers have mentioned this fruit.

[[Saki]] uses medlars in his [[short stories]], which often play on the decay of Edwardian society.  In "The Peace of Mowsle Barton", the outwardly quiet farmstead features a medlar tree and corrosive hatred.  In "The Boar Pig", the titular animal, [[Tarquinius Superbus|Tarquin Superbus]], is the point of contact between society ladies cheating to get into ''the'' [[garden party]] of the season and a not entirely honest young schoolgirl who lures him away by strategically throwing well-bletted medlars: "Come, Tarquin, dear old boy; you know you can't resist medlars when they're rotten and squashy."

Italian novelist [[Giovanni Verga]]'s naturalist narrative ''I Malavoglia'' is titled ''The House by the Medlar Tree'' in the English translation.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/The-House-by-the-Medlar-Tree | title=The House by the Medlar Tree {{!}} novel by Verga |encyclopedia=Britannica }}</ref>

[[H. C. Bailey]]'s detective Reggie Fortune is very fond of medlars.{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}}

[[Philip Pullman]] describes Sir Charles Latrom's perfume as "rotted like a medlar" in his book ''The Subtle Knife''.
